title: The Budha Dal today
hook: the Nihang army traces itself to the elders' Dal of this century

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Ardas: it names the martyrs, not the enemies, and asks the good of all. Courage, not revenge. Today, riders who never left the saddle.

Deep blue robes. A turban wound high, almost a tower, ringed with steel circles and small blades. A spear in hand, a horse nearby, a voice calling out the Khalsa's victory cry. If you've seen photographs from the festival of Hola Mohalla at Anandpur, you may have seen them: the Nihangs. They can look like figures stepped out of an old painting. They aren't a reenactment. They say they are the same army that rode through the century you've been hearing about, still riding. Today: the Budha Dal today.
screen: `BLUE ROBES, A TOWERING TURBAN.` → `HOLA MOHALLA AT ANANDPUR.` → `THE SAME ARMY, STILL RIDING.`

segments.voice: A few weeks back on this path, the Khalsa organized its riders into two bodies: the Budha Dal, the army of the elders, and the Taruna Dal, the army of the young. Budha means old. The elders' Dal kept the camps, guarded the shrines, held the memory. The Nihang groups of today trace themselves to that body. One still carries the name Budha Dal, with its own jathedar, its own leader, and its own camps that move from place to place. In their telling, the line was never broken. Second, what they keep. Tradition says the Nihangs hold on to ways of the old riders that life elsewhere has left behind: the blue dress, the high turban with its weapons, moving camps, care for horses, the martial art called gatka, and a coded, joking way of speaking that belongs to the camps. Time with them shows the hard century as a practice, not a chapter. Third, honest complexity. There's more than one Nihang Dal today, and they don't all agree, with each other or with other Sikhs, about every practice. Sikhs hold a range of views about them. What's clear is the claim they make: the riders of the hard century didn't only leave descendants and stories. They left an army that still keeps its camp. The old army lives.
screen: `BUDHA DAL: THE ARMY OF THE ELDERS.` · `NIHANGS TRACE THEMSELVES TO IT.` · `BLUE DRESS, GATKA, MOVING CAMPS.` · `MORE THAN ONE DAL, MORE THAN ONE VIEW.` · then, large: `THE OLD ARMY LIVES.`

segments.voice: Bring up an old way kept alive by someone you know: a recipe made the old way, a song sung only at weddings, a craft still done by hand. Picture them keeping it, and notice how easily it could have stopped with them. Rest there in gratitude, with Waheguru on each breath out if you pray.
Nihang. The order of Sikh warriors who say they are the elders' army of the hard century still riding: blue robes, high turbans, moving camps. Today's word.
Your line: the old army lives. Some history is still on horseback. Day eight hundred seventy-eight, done.

howItsDone: Nihang Sikhs live in Dals with their own leaders and moving camps, wear blue with high turbans, keep horses and practice gatka, and gather for Hola Mohalla at Anandpur.

fork.setup: you're a rider in the elders' Dal. the hard century ends, the land is settled, and the war is over. what happens to your Dal?
options: it disbands, and everyone goes home to farm.
it keeps its camp, its dress and its ways, and carries them on.
it becomes a regular government army.
fork.reveal: the Nihangs of the Budha Dal say their camp never broke up: they still keep the dress, the horses and the moving camps of the old riders.

original.note: Gurmukhi for Nihang, the name of the Sikh order that keeps the old Dals.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Budha Dal is a chapter in a history book.

what a scholar hears: one Nihang body still carries the name Budha Dal with its own jathedar, and the Nihangs are a living link to the practice of the hard century, though several Dals exist and views about them vary.

chat.says: I saw Sikhs in blue robes and tall turbans at Hola Mohalla. Are they actors?

They're the one army all Sikhs follow, and every Sikh agrees about how they live.
